The biblical canon

Reformed sources · Reformed sources and authority

The biblical canon

5 sectionsNot completed
Notes

The biblical canon is the recognized collection of scriptural books. These readings show that older Christian book lists and modern confessional classifications need careful attention. St. Philaret’s distinction between listed books and books appointed for instruction should be read in his own terminology rather than assumed to match Westminster’s categories exactly.[1][2][3]

How does Westminster classify the Apocrypha?[1]

Westminster excludes the books it calls Apocrypha from the inspired scriptural canon. It therefore gives them no distinct authority in the Church beyond other human writings. This is the confession’s explicit classification.[1]

Read original passage

Westminster: the books called Apocrypha

The books commonly called Apocrypha, not being of divine inspiration, are no part of the canon of the Scripture, and therefore are of no authority in the church of God, nor to be any otherwise approved, or made use of, than other human writings.

How does St. Philaret discuss Old Testament book lists?[2]

St. Philaret gives a twenty-two-part reckoning associated with St. Cyril and St. Athanasius and explains some books as combined units. The number alone does not tell a reader how modern individual book titles are counted. He also distinguishes books absent from Hebrew from the listed books and cites St. Athanasius on their use in instruction for people entering the Church.[2]

Read original passage

Philaret: Old Testament books

32. Why should we attend to the reckoning of the Hebrews?

Because, as the Apostle Paul says, unto them were committed the oracles of God; and the sacred books of the Old Testament have been received from the Hebrew Church of that Testament by the Christian Church of the New. Rom. iii. 2.

33. How do St. Cyril and St. Athanasius enumerate the books of the Old Testament?

As follows: 1, The book of Genesis; 2, Exodus; 3, Leviticus; 4, the book of Numbers; 5, Deuteronomy; 6, the book of Jesus the son of Nun; 7, the book of Judges, and with it, as an appendix, the book of Ruth; 8, the first and second books of Kings, as two parts of one book; 9, the third and fourth books of Kings; 10, the first and second books of Paralipomena; 11, the first book of Esdras, and the second, or, as it is entitled in Greek, the book of Nehemiah; 12, the book of Esther; 13, the book of Job; 14, the Psalms; 15, the Proverbs of Solomon; 16, Ecclesiastes, also by Solomon; 17, the Song of Songs, also by Solomon; 18, the book of the Prophet Isaiah; 19, of Jeremiah; 20, of Ezekiel; 21, of Daniel; 22, of the Twelve Prophets.

34. Why is there no notice taken in this enumeration of the books of the Old Testament of the book of the Wisdom of the son of Sirach, and of certain others?

Because they do not exist in the Hebrew.

35. How are we to regard these last-named books?

Athanasius the Great says that they have been appointed of the Fathers to be read by proselytes who are preparing for admission into the Church.

St. Athanasius’s own list and distinctions[3]

Festal Letter 39 is linked as a primary source for St. Athanasius’s enumeration and his distinction concerning books for reading. Its complete sections provide context beyond St. Philaret’s reference to him.[3]
